**Title:** "Linguistic Strategies for Improving Informed Consent in Clinical Trials Among Low Health Literacy Patients"

**Authors:** Janice L. Krieger (corresponding), Jordan M. Neil, Yulia A. Strekalova, Melanie A. Sarge

**Year:** 2016 (published 2016-10-14)

**Venue/Journal:** *JNCI Journal of the National Cancer Institute*, vol. 109, issue 3, article djw233 (Oxford University Press)

**DOI:** 10.1093/jnci/djw233 | **PMID:** 27794035

**Publication type:** Peer-reviewed journal article (hybrid open access, CC-BY-NC)

**Key findings (sample size: 500 cancer patients):**
- Post-test-only experimental design; participants were randomly assigned to one of three message conditions explaining randomization (plain language, gambling metaphor, benign metaphor) or a control message.
- "Health literacy was a statistically significant moderator of randomization comprehension (P = .03)."
- Among participants with the lowest health literacy, the benign metaphor resulted in greater comprehension than plain language (P = .04) or the gambling metaphor (P = .004).
- Conversely, at the highest health literacy level, the benign metaphor was associated with lower comprehension (P = .04).
- A serial mediation model showed a negative indirect effect on behavioral intention via personal relevance of RCTs and anxiety about participation (P < .001).
- Conclusion: metaphor effectiveness depends on health literacy â€” the benign metaphor worked particularly well for those at the lower end of the spectrum â€” and the findings offer guidance on how future communication research should improve informed consent processes.

## Bibliographic Record

**Title:** "Poor writing, not specialized concepts, drives processing difficulty in legal language"

**Authors:** Eric MartĂ­nez (MIT), Francis Mollica (University of Edinburgh), Edward Gibson (MIT)

**Year:** 2022 (published March 4, 2022; preprint on PsyArXiv 2021)

**Venue/Journal:** *Cognition*, vol. 224, article 105070 (Elsevier)

**DOI:** 10.1016/j.cognition.2022.105070 (PMID: 35257980)

**Publication type:** Peer-reviewed journal article (open access, hybrid, CC BY-NC-ND)

---

**Key findings:**

- A corpus analysis of ~10 million words found contracts contain "startlingly high proportions" of hard-to-process features â€” low-frequency jargon, center-embedded clauses, passive voice, and non-standard capitalization â€” compared with nine other written and spoken English genres.
- Two experiments (**N = 184**) showed that excerpts containing these features were "recalled and comprehended at lower rates" than versions without them, even among experienced readers.
- The results undermine the "specialized concepts" account of legal theory: difficulty is attributed mainly to working-memory limits imposed by long-distance syntactic dependencies, i.e., poor writing, rather than a lack of technical legal knowledge.
- The authors conclude that editing out these features would be tractable and beneficial for society.

## Summary

**Article identification:** The paper is **"Bot or not: Can people tell the difference between stories written by a human or by an AI system?"** by **Sydney Sears and Dr. Deena Skolnick Weisberg** (Villanova University), published online August 5 in the journal ***Judgment and Decision Making*** (Cambridge University Press). Note: the search results do not explicitly list a DOI, but the article is available at the Cambridge Core link: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/judgment-and-decision-making/article/bot-or-not-can-people-tell-the-difference-between-stories-written-by-a-human-or-by-an-ai-system/45E6DC0BB90AA648654D5AE243F6C667

**Study design:** 2,587 U.S. participants took part in three experiments. The researchers pitted three short stories published in established literary journals against three similar stories generated using OpenAI's ChatGPT 4.0.

**Key findings:**

1. **People cannot reliably distinguish AI from human writing.** When participants were asked to identify which of two stories was human-written, only **39.4% guessed correctly** in one experiment, and performance was effectively random (**52%**) in another run months later when more people had been exposed to AI. The authors concluded: "There is no general evidence that participants were able to distinguish human-written from AI-generated stories."

2. **People actually prefer AI-generated stories when blind to authorship.** In the first experiment, readers judged AI-generated fiction as superior in quality and more absorbing than human-written counterparts.

3. **Algorithm aversion emerges when authorship is revealed.** When participants were told a story was "human-written," they rated it higher regardless of its true origin â€” a "textbook case of algorithm aversion." The authors summarized: "People actually prefer AI-generated stories while believing that these stories are worse."

**Proposed explanations:** AI fiction tends to be more fluent and easier to comprehend, more emotionally upbeat than human texts, and language models smooth over individual quirks (a regression-to-the-mean effect). People who relied on cues like language style and personal enjoyment tended to guess incorrectly. However, participants with greater familiarity with AI tools were more likely to correctly identify AI-generated work.

**Context/limitations:** The study extends prior work showing people struggle to distinguish AI from human poetry and that "algorithm aversion" leads to devaluation of AI-labeled creative work. The study was limited to short stories (~5 minutes to read), leaving open whether AI can sustain quality over a full novel.

## Summary

**Bibliographic details (as requested in the query):**

- **Title:** "A Survey on LLM-Generated Text Detection: Necessity, Methods, and Future Directions"
- **Authors:** Junchao Wu, Shu Yang, Runzhe Zhan, Yulin Yuan, Lidia Sam Chao, and Derek Fai Wong
- **Journal:** *Computational Linguistics* (MIT Press), Volume 51, Issue 1
- **Pages:** 275â€“338
- **Publication date:** March 2025 (published 15 March 2025)
- **DOI:** **10.1162/coli_a_00549** (also given as http://dx.doi.org/10.1162/coli_a_00549)

**Overview of the paper's content (from the abstract):**

The survey addresses the urgent need for detection mechanisms to identify LLM-generated text, given how rapidly large language models have integrated AI-generated content into daily life and the risks of misuse in domains such as artistic expression and social networks. It frames LLM-generated text detection as a binary classification task (determining whether a given text was produced by an LLM) and consolidates recent research breakthroughs, including:

- **Detection methods:** watermarking techniques, statistics-based detectors, neural-based detectors, and human-assisted methods.
- **Datasets:** a review of existing datasets, their limitations, and developmental requirements.
- **Challenges:** out-of-distribution problems, potential attacks, real-world data issues, and ineffective evaluation frameworks.
- **Future directions:** research avenues to advance responsible artificial intelligence in LLM-generated text detection.

The survey aims to serve as both a comprehensive introduction for newcomers and a source of valuable updates for seasoned researchers in the field.

## Paper Metadata

- **Title:** Human Bias in the Face of AI: Examining Human Judgment Against Text Labeled as AI Generated
- **Authors:** Tiffany Zhu, Iain Weissburg, Kexun Zhang, and William Yang Wang
- **Year:** 2025 (July)
- **Venue:** Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025 (Vienna, Austria)
- **Pages:** 25907â€“25914
- **DOI:** 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.1329

## Key Experimental Findings

The study ran three experiments (text rephrasing, news article summarization, and persuasive writing) in which human raters judged labeled and unlabeled content. The main results:

- In blind tests, raters could not reliably tell AI-generated text apart from human-written text.
- However, when labels were attached, raters showed a strong bias: they "overwhelmingly favored content labeled as 'Human Generated,'" over AI-labeled content, by a "preference score of over 30%."
- Crucially, the same pattern held even when the labels were deliberately swapped â€” meaning the raters were reacting to the label itself, not the actual source of the text.

The authors interpret this as a human bias against AI that "undervalues AI performance," with broader societal and cognitive implications, and they position the work as a foundation for improving human-AI collaboration, especially in creative fields.

**Authors:** Weixin Liang, Yaohui Zhang, Zhengxuan Wu, Haley Lepp, Wenlong Ji, Xuandong Zhao, Hancheng Cao, Sheng Liu, Siyu He, Zhi Huang, Diyi Yang, Christopher Potts, Christopher D. Manning, and James Y. Zou (most affiliated with Stanford University, with Zhao at UC Santa Barbara).

**Key findings:** The study conducted a systematic analysis of 1,121,912 preprints and published papers from January 2020 to September 2024 across arXiv, bioRxiv, and Nature portfolio journals, using a population-level framework based on word frequency shifts to estimate the prevalence of LLM-modified content over time. Results showed a steady increase in LLM usage in scientific writing, with the largest and fastest growth estimated for computer science papers (up to 22%). By comparison, mathematics papers and the Nature portfolio showed lower evidence of LLM modification (up to 9%). LLM modification estimates were higher among papers from first authors who post preprints more frequently, papers in more crowded research areas, and shorter papers. The authors concluded that LLMs are being broadly used in scientific writing.

# KLEJ: Comprehensive Benchmark for Polish Language Understanding (Rybak et al., ACL 2020)

**KLEJ** is a comprehensive multi-task benchmark for Polish language understanding, introduced by Piotr Rybak, Robert Mroczkowski, Janusz Tracz, and Ireneusz Gawlik at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020), held online in July 2020 (pages 1191â€“1201; DOI: 10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.111; arXiv:2005.00630, submitted May 1, 2020).

## Motivation
The authors note that while Transformer-based models drove major improvements in natural language understanding (NLU) and general NLU benchmarks enable fair comparison of methods, such benchmarks existed only for a handful of languages. KLEJ was created to address this gap for Polish.

## Key Features
- **Multi-task benchmark**: Comprises a diverse set of tasks adopted from existing datasets, covering named entity recognition, question-answering, textual entailment, and others.
- **New task introduced**: The Allegro Reviews (AR) sentiment analysis task for the e-commerce domain.
- **Domain diversity**: Includes datasets from varying domains and applications to ensure a common evaluation scheme and promote models that generalize across different NLU tasks.
- **Online leaderboard**: The benchmark is accompanied by an online leaderboard for tracking model performance.

## HerBERT Model
The authors released **HerBERT**, a Transformer-based model trained specifically for Polish. It achieved the best average performance across the benchmark and obtained the best results for three out of nine tasks.

## Evaluation
The paper provides extensive evaluation results comparing several standard baselines and recently proposed multilingual Transformer-based models.

## Citation
Rybak, Piotr, Robert Mroczkowski, Janusz Tracz, and Ireneusz Gawlik. 2020. "KLEJ: Comprehensive Benchmark for Polish Language Understanding." In *Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics*, pages 1191â€“1201, Online. Association for Computational Linguistics.

- **Title:** "Demystifying the First-Time Experience of Mobile Games: The Presence of a Tutorial Has a Positive Impact on Non-Expert Players' Flow and Continuous-Use Intentions"
- **Authors:** Mario Passalacqua (Polytechnique MontrĂ©al); RaphaĂ«l Morin, Sylvain SĂ©nĂ©cal, Pierre-Majorique LĂ©ger (HEC MontrĂ©al); Lennart E. Nacke (University of Waterloo)
- **Year:** 2020 (published July 11, 2020)
- **Venue/Journal:** *Multimodal Technologies and Interaction*, Vol. 4, Issue 3, Article 41 (MDPI; open access, CC-BY)
- **DOI:** 10.3390/mti4030041
- **Publication type:** Peer-reviewed journal article
- **Funding:** Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (CRSNG EGP 484281-15)

## Key Findings

The study used a laboratory experiment with **40 players** to test how tutorial presence and player expertise affect psychophysiological states and continuous-use intentions (CUIs). The research context is mobile game retention, where many players abandon games "within 24 h of downloading them."

Main results:
- In a simple game context, "tutorials have a positive impact on non-expert players' perceived state of flow," but showed **no effect on expert players' flow**.
- Tutorials had a **positive effect on continuous-use intentions (CUIs) for both experts and non-experts**.

The authors position this as relevant to game design decisions â€” suggesting tutorials can facilitate early engagement and help non-expert players reach a flow state, while not harming expert players' experience and boosting retention intentions across both groups.

**Authors:** Tom Kocmi, Tomasz Limisiewicz, Gabriel Stanovsky

**Year:** 2020

**Title:** Gender Coreference and Bias Evaluation at WMT 2020

**Venue:** The provided page does not explicitly state the publication venue; it is an arXiv preprint (arXiv:2010.06018) reporting evaluation of systems submitted to the WMT 2020 News shared task.

**Polish-specific findings:** The authors extended the WinoMT test suite to Polish (and Czech), covering 3,136 Polish test examples. All evaluated systems performed better on male than female professions (positive Î”G, e.g., up to 50.3 for zlabs-nlp) and substantially better on stereotypical than anti-stereotypical gender roles (positive Î”S). Notably, for 16 professions lacking common feminine derivations (e.g., mechanic, veterinarian, engineer), "the female gender was correctly assigned in only 1.5% of the translations." In some cases, systems inserted a gender-marking word like "pani" ("mrs.") before the masculine occupation name, which the evaluators counted as correct. The Polish morphological analyser achieved 98.8% accuracy against human annotation, and the whitelist approach failed on only 1,533 of 47,267 examples.

## Summary

**"Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary"** is a paper by Dmitry Kobak, Rita GonzĂˇlez-MĂˇrquez, EmĹ‘ke-Ă�gnes HorvĂˇt, and Jan Lause, published in *Science Advances* (2025, Vol. 11, Issue 27, article eadt3813; DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adt3813; published online July 2, 2025, print July 4, 2025).

**Objective and approach:** The authors sought to quantify how widespread LLM usage is in biomedical scholarly writing. They analyzed vocabulary changes in more than 15 million biomedical abstracts indexed by PubMed from 2010 to 2024. To quantify word-frequency increases, they computed a "counterfactual expected frequency" for 2024 based on linear extrapolation of 2021â€“2022 frequencies (deliberately excluding 2023 data, which might already be LLM-affected). Two complementary measures were used: the **excess frequency gap** Î´ = p â�’ q (empirical minus expected frequency), which highlights excess usage of frequent words, and the **excess frequency ratio** r = p/q, which highlights infrequent words.

**Key findings:**
- Across 26,657 words, many showed strong excess usage in 2024. Less common words with strong excess usage included *delves* (r = 28.0), *underscores* (r = 13.8), and *showcasing* (r = 10.7); more common words included *potential* (Î´ = 0.052), *findings* (Î´ = 0.041), and *crucial* (Î´ = 0.037).
- For comparison (2013â€“2023), no single word showed an excess frequency gap Î´ > 0.01 from 2013 to 2019. During the COVID pandemic (2020â€“2022), words like *coronavirus*, *covid*, *lockdown*, and *pandemic* showed very large excess usages (up to r > 1000 and Î´ = 0.06) â€” but these were overwhelmingly **content words** (e.g., *respiratory*, *remdesivir*), mostly nouns (79.2%).
- In contrast, the 2024 excess vocabulary consisted almost entirely of **style words**: of 379 excess style words, 66% were verbs and 14% were adjectives (e.g., *intricate*, *notably*). The number of excess words rose to 454 in 2024 (343 unique lemmas), roughly one year after ChatGPT's release â€” surpassing the COVID-era peak of 190 words in 2021.

**Main estimate of LLM usage:** Combining excess style words as markers, the authors computed lower bounds on LLM usage. For example, Î´ = 0.052 for *potential* suggests at least 5.2% of 2024 abstracts went through an LLM. Combining words raised this bound: using two independent marker sets (an automatically generated "rare set" of 291 low-frequency excess style words, and a manually curated "common set" of high-Î´ words), both approaches converged on a robust estimate. The analysis suggests that **at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs**, with the lower bound varying across disciplines, countries, and journals â€” reaching **40% for some subcorpora**.

**Conclusion:** LLMs have had an unprecedented impact on scientific writing in biomedical research, surpassing the effect of major world events such as the COVID pandemic. The paper's analysis code and data are publicly available in the GitHub repository `berenslab/llm-excess-vocab` (including all 900 excess words identified from 2013â€“2024 with annotations, yearly word counts, and a t-SNE visualization of 2022â€“2024 abstracts). # Ĺšmigiel Dataset â€” Machine-Generated Text Detection in Polish (LREC-COLING 2025 / ACL Anthology)

## What it is
**Ĺšmigiel** is the first open dataset for training and evaluating **machine-generated text (MGT) detection in Polish**. It was introduced in the paper *"Ĺšmigiel Dataset: Laying Foundations for Investigating Machine-Generated Text Detection in Polish"* by **Jakub Strebeyko (University of Warsaw), Alina WrĂłblewska, and Piotr PrzybyĹ‚a (Institute of Computer Science, Polish Academy of Sciences)**, published at **LREC 2025 (LREC-COLING 2025)**, year 2025. It is available on Hugging Face as `strebeyko/smigiel` and on GitHub as `poleval/2025-smigiel`.

## Dataset composition
- **Human-written texts** from multiple domains (the GitHub repo lists customer reviews, literature, social media, and Wikipedia; the paper abstract cites six domains), used to prompt text generation.
- **Machine-generated texts** produced by **eight language models** capable of generating credible Polish text (including Llama 3.1 8B, Bielik 7B/11B, Mistral 7B/Nemo, PLLuM 12B, and larger models).
- The **raw corpus contains over 462K generated texts**, plus a **cleaned, source- and domain-balanced subset of 64,538 human-written and machine-generated texts** suitable for training and benchmarking MGT detectors.
- Preliminary experiments showed detection difficulty depends on text domain, generating model, and training-data similarity; general-purpose classifiers generalize to new LLMs but struggle with genres unseen in training.

## PolEval 2025 shared task (ACL Anthology)
The dataset was originally created for **Shared Task 1 at PolEval 2025**, described in the paper *"PolEval 2025 Task 1 Ĺšmigiel: Spotting Machine-Generated Text from LLMs for Polish"* (PrzybyĹ‚a, Strebeyko, WrĂłblewska), published in the **Proceedings of the PolEval 2025 Workshop**, **ACL Anthology ID: 2025.poleval-main.2**, pages 5â€“15, Warsaw (Institute of Computer Science PAS and Association for Computational Linguistics, November 2025). Key results:
- **Three scenarios**: unsupervised, constrained (training only on the provided dataset), and open (any external data).
- **Seven systems** were submitted; the best constrained systems exceeded **90% accuracy** on the main evaluation set.
- Accuracy **dropped on unseen domains and unseen generator models**, revealing generalization limits; in the most challenging settings, **unsupervised approaches outperformed supervised ones**.

## Related system papers in the same workshop volume (2025.poleval-main)
- **2025.poleval-main.3** â€” *"Detecting Machine-Generated Text in Polish Using Fine-Tuned Qwen Models"* (Konrad PierzyĹ„ski).
- **2025.poleval-main.4** â€” *"Perplexity-Driven Contrastive Scoring for Unsupervised Detection of AI-Generated Texts in Polish"* (Damian Stachura), which adapted the Binoculars detector with Polish-trained language models and calibrated thresholds, achieving **first place in the zero-shot track** (code: github.com/damian1996/2025-smigiel). Another entry evaluated 91 model pairs using character-level perplexity differences, identifying Gemma-3-27B + PLLuM-12B as optimal (81.22% accuracy on unseen generators).

# Summary: Kobak et al., "Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary" (Science Advances)

## Note on the query identifier
The identifier "sciadv.adn2496" does not appear anywhere in the search results. All results correspond to the paper published as **Science Advances 11(27), eadt3813 (2025), DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adt3813** â€” i.e., Dmitry Kobak, Rita GonzĂˇlez-MĂˇrquez, EmĹ‘ke-Ă�gnes HorvĂˇt, and Jan Lause, *"Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary"* (published online July 2, 2025; corresponding author Dmitry Kobak, Hertie Institute for AI in Brain Health, University of TĂĽbingen). This is the "excess vocabulary" / Kobak / Science Advances paper matching the rest of the query.

## Method
- The authors adapted the COVID-era "excess deaths" epidemiological framework (previously used by Kobak for the World Mortality Dataset) to an **"excess word" analysis**.
- They analyzed vocabulary changes in **more than 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010â€“2024** indexed in PubMed (15.1 million abstracts in one account).
- For each word, they calculated a counterfactual expected 2024 frequency based on linear extrapolation of 2021â€“2022 frequencies (deliberately excluding 2023, which could already be affected by LLMs), then computed two complementary measures of excess usage: the **excess frequency gap Î´ = p â�’ q** (good for frequent words) and the **excess frequency ratio r = p/q** (good for infrequent words).

## Key findings
- **454 excess words in 2024** (vs. up to 190 in 2021 during COVID), roughly one year after ChatGPT's release; counting unique lemmas only, **343 unique lemmas in 2024 vs. 180 in 2021**.
- All 900 unique excess words from 2013â€“2024 were manually annotated: 51.3% content words, 45.2% style words. **COVID-era excess vocabulary was almost entirely content words** (e.g., *respiratory*, *remdesivir*), whereas **2024 excess vocabulary was almost entirely style words**. Before 2024, excess words were predominantly nouns (79.2%); in 2024, of 379 excess style words, **66% were verbs and 14% adjectives**.
- Examples: less common words with strong excess usage included **delves (r = 28.0), underscores (r = 13.8), showcasing (r = 10.7)**; more common words included **potential (Î´ = 0.052), findings (Î´ = 0.041), crucial (Î´ = 0.037)**. Later-2024 excess words also included *heighten*, *hinder*, *unparalleled*, and *invaluable* (a full list of ~291 rare excess style words is in the supplementary materials).
- Historical comparison: from 2013â€“2019 no single word ever showed Î´ > 0.01; the COVID pandemic (2020â€“2022) brought words like *coronavirus*, *covid*, *lockdown*, *pandemic* with r > 1000 and Î´ = 0.06.
- **Lower-bound estimate: at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs** (corresponding to ~200,000 of ~1.5 million 2024 PubMed abstracts). This lower bound varied by discipline, country, and journal, **reaching 40% for some subcorpora**; usage was higher in China and South Korea, in computer science and bioinformatics, and in MDPI and Frontiers journals (>1/5 of abstracts).
- The authors conclude LLMs have had an **unprecedented impact on scientific writing in biomedical research, surpassing the effect of major world events such as the COVID pandemic**.
- The preprint version (arXiv:2406.07016, June 2024) had estimated ~1/9 of first-half-2024 abstracts showed LLM-writing signs, indicating accelerating adoption.

## Code, data, and reception
- Analysis code and data are openly available on GitHub at **berenslab/llm-excess-vocab** (MIT license): all 900 excess words with annotations (`results/excess_words.csv`), yearly word counts, figures, and full reproducibility instructions; an update (July 2025) adds six more months of PubMed data and monthly excess values.
- The paper had ~161 citations on Semantic Scholar, with follow-up work extending the approach to other fields (e.g., astronomy, ophthalmology, engineering) and full texts.

# Summary: "I, ChatGPT: Linguistic Properties and Human Experiences of Human- versus AI-Generated Stories"

**Publication details:** The study was published in *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications* (2025, Vol. 12, Issue 1, pp. 1â€“11), authored by Markus Appel (University of WĂĽrzburg), Wojciech P. Malecki (University of WrocĹ‚aw), Tanja V. Messingschlager, and Julia R. Winkler.

**Research question and design:** The paper investigates whether AI-generated stories differ from human-authored stories in their linguistic properties and in how readers experience them. The study comprised two experiments:

- **Study 1:** ChatGPT and 100 non-professional human authors (students) were asked to create stories based on similar prompts, producing a pool of 200 stories.
- **Study 2:** 380 naĂŻve participants were randomly assigned to read either an AI-generated or a human-written story from that pool.

**Key findings â€” linguistic properties:** Linguistic analyses revealed that ChatGPT-generated stories contained **fewer personal pronouns** and **fewer descriptions of relativity** (words indicating space, time, and motion) than human stories, but **more positive emotions**.

**Key findings â€” reader experiences:** In Study 2, **no differences were found in novelty or entertainment experiences** between AI- and human-generated stories. However, **readers of AI stories were significantly less transported into the story world** (i.e., lower narrative transportation). Mediation analyses showed that this reduced transportation could be attributed specifically to **ChatGPT's less frequent use of personal pronouns**, which are important for clarifying narrative perspective and familiarizing readers with characters.

**Theoretical context:** The authors note that personal pronouns help establish the story's perspective and contribute to narrative transportation, emotional responses intensify narrative experiences, and relativity and perceptual-process words aid readers in constructing mental models of the story world. They also discuss whether AI can match human storytelling, noting that while AI can perform sentiment analysis, it has yet to demonstrate sophisticated emotional understanding, and AI stories may lack the poignant, bittersweet moments that elicit eudaimonic (meaningful) entertainment experiences. The paper concludes that whether AI can outperform humans at storytelling must be established empirically.

**Related context in the search results:** A separate 2025 study led by Dr. James O'Sullivan at University College Cork, also published in *Nature â€“ Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*, used literary stylometry to compare human and AI creative prose, finding that AI writing (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 70B) displays a "detectable stylistic fingerprint" â€” compact, uniform patterns â€” whereas human writing shows far greater variation and idiosyncrasy. (Note: This is a distinct study from the Appel et al. paper.) Additionally, the search results include an unrelated creative work, a novel titled *I, ChatGPT* by Nikola MarkoviÄ‡, which is not the academic study in question.

## Summary

The search results identify the paper **"Form Without Function? Register Sensitivity in CEFRâ€�Conditioned LLM and Secondâ€�Language Learner Writing"** by Michele Carlo and Osamu Takeuchi, published as a research article in the *International Journal of Applied Linguistics* (Wiley, 2026, pp. 1â€“17; DOI: 10.1111/ijal.70284).

**Research question and design:** The study investigated whether large language models (LLMs) can generate text that resembles second-language (L2) learner writing at requested proficiency levels *and* adapts to communicative contexts the way human learners do. The researchers compared LLM-generated and human L2 writing across three task-defined categories (informalâ€“personal, semi-formalâ€“expository, formalâ€“argumentative) and four CEFR levels (A2â€“C1), using Biber's multi-dimensional analysis (MDA). Six instruction-tuned LLMs responded to Write & Improve prompts (n = 592 human texts; n = 4,724 LLM texts), with the EFCAMDAT corpus serving as the human baseline.

**Key findings:**
- Under CEFR-only prompting, LLM outputs shifted on MDA dimensions tied to **informational density and explicitness**, but showed **weaker, differently directed, or less variable differentiation** on dimensions tied to **persuasion and elaboration**, particularly in formalâ€“argumentative tasks.
- The **largest gap between LLM and human writing occurred at the C1 level**, where CEFR descriptors most emphasize register flexibility.
- LLM outputs were **more uniform than human writing** and clustered near the center of the human distributional space, showing less variation than authentic learner texts.
- This broad pattern **recurred across all six model families** tested.

**Conclusion:** CEFR-conditioned generation can reproduce some structural signals of proficiency while showing limited human-like register differentiation in MDA spaceâ€”a pattern the authors interpret as **"form without function"** (i.e., the surface forms of proficiency are present, but the functional, context-adaptive register variation of human learners is lacking).

tool_input.prompt: Give the exact author, year, volume/issue, pages and DOI of this LingVaria article about the linguistic correctness of AI-generated texts (ChatGPT) in Polish. Summarize its method and findings briefly.

tool_response.result:
**Bibliographic details:** Mazur, R. (2024), "O poprawnoĹ›ci jÄ™zykowej tekstĂłw generowanych przez SI na przykĹ‚adzie ChatuGPT", *LingVaria*, 19(1(37)), pp. 119â€“138. DOI: [10.12797/LV.19.2024.37.08](https://doi.org/10.12797/LV.19.2024.37.08)

**Method:** The study assessed the linguistic accuracy of ChatGPT-generated Polish texts using prompts modeled on the 2023 Polish secondary school final exam (matura) in Polish language and literature. The author identified, classified, and counted language errors in the outputs.

**Findings:** Accuracy varied across texts. As the abstract states, "Most errors occurred in texts containing more complex constructions," where correct formulation required a thorough grasp of grammatical rules. The conclusions point to limitations of AI that users should keep in mind when editing chatbot-generated texts.

**Article details** (from the journal page):

- **Author:** Karolina Zuchewicz (UniversitĂ¤t Leipzig)
- **Year:** 2024 (published 31-12-2024)
- **Source:** *LingBaW. Linguistics Beyond and Within*, Vol. 10, pp. 265â€“281
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.31743/lingbaw.18023
- **Citation as given:** "Zuchewicz, K. (2024). Aspect and pragmatics in Polish with a view to Sorbian. LingBaW. Linguistics Beyond and Within, 10, 265â€“281."

**Abstract summary:** The paper examines perfective aspect meaning in Polish through "general-factual contexts" (references to completed events). Slavic languages vary in aspect choice here: East Slavic speakers "mostly choose the imperfective aspect," while West Slavic speakers face "a stronger competition between imperfective and perfective forms." The author applies the notion of "pragmatic contract" (from Israeli 1996 for Russian), arguing that a contract's presence favors the perfective and its absence favors the imperfective. She proposes that this contract does not affect aspectual distribution in Upper Sorbian, which "point[s] to a difference in the aspectual systems of the two West Slavic languages and confirming the status of Polish as transitional between East and West Slavic."

**NKJP corpus use:** Yes. The abstract states the assumptions "are verified with data from the Narodowy Korpus JÄ™zyka Polskiego (PrzepiĂłrkowski et al. 2012)."

**The paper in question:** Miechowicz-Mathiasen and Scheffler's "A corpus-based analysis of the peculiar behaviour of the Polish verb *podobaÄ‡ siÄ™*" (Katarzyna Miechowicz-Mathiasen & PaweĹ‚ Scheffler, published in *Elements of Slavic and Germanic Grammars: A Comparative View*, eds. J. WitkoĹ› & G. Fanselow, Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang, 2008, pp. 89â€“111; also listed as a 2012 conference paper) is a corpus-based microstudy of the Polish psych-verb *podobaÄ‡ siÄ™* ('to please/like').

**Key findings and claims from the available snippets:**

- **Psych-verb classification:** *PodobaÄ‡ siÄ™* is treated as a psych-verb whose syntactic behaviour resembles the PIACERE-class of psych-verbs proposed by Belletti & Rizzi (1988). The paper works within generative frameworks where syntactic configurations and semantic (thematic) information are interrelated.

- **Word order alternations:** The paper addresses the alternating word orders of the verb's arguments. The snippets illustrate raising constructions with both orders â€” Dative Experiencer before Nominative Theme and vice versa:
  - *Janowi (DAT) zdaje siÄ™ podobaÄ‡ mĂłj dom (NOM)* â€“ 'John seems to like my house'
  - *MĂłj dom (NOM) zdaje siÄ™ podobaÄ‡ Janowi (DAT)*
  - These are paralleled with Italian *piacere* constructions (e.g., *A Gianni sembra piacere questa casa* / *Questa casa sembra piacere a Gianni*).

- **Proposed analysis:** The authors propose that alternating verbs of the *piacere*-class are unaccusative in the sense of lacking an external argument, drawing substantially on Belletti & Rizzi (1988). However, they explicitly **disagree with B&R that both arguments of these verbs follow the verb**, instead allowing for the pre-verbal spell-out of either argument (the DAT or NOM argument can appear first).

- **Theoretical context:** The paper discusses and rejects alternative approaches, including the Aspectual Interface Hypothesis (Tenny 1994) and Pesetsky's (1995) theta-role-based account (Causer vs. Target/Subject Matter roles), arguing these are not fully appropriate for *piacere*-class alternating verbs.

# Excluding sponsored, predatory, and non-scholarly sources

The goal of this repository is evidence, not persuasion. Screen out anything
whose purpose is to sell, rank, or promote rather than to report findings.

## Never use as evidence of fact

- **Sponsored / "partner" / "paid" content** and native advertising.
- **Press releases and PR wire** (PR Newswire, Business Wire, EurekAlert item
  reproduced uncritically) â€” trace to the underlying paper instead.
- **Vendor blogs, product pages, whitepapers, case studies** â€” marketing.
- **SEO listicles / "best of" affiliate content** ("Top 10 â€¦", comparison sites
  monetised by referrals).
- **Op-eds, editorials, opinion columns, personal blogs, social media.**
- **AI-generated content farms** and aggregators that don't link primary sources.

These may be *quoted as objects of study* ("Company X claims Y"), but never
counted as evidence that the claim is true. Always mark them as such.

## Predatory / low-quality journal red flags

A source being in a "journal" is not enough. Watch for:

- Not indexed in **DOAJ**, **Scopus**, **Web of Science**, **PubMed/MEDLINE**,
  or the relevant field database.
- Publisher on cautionary lists / not a member of **COPE**, **OASPA**, or
  **WAME**; missing from **Think-Check-Submit** style checks.
- Fake or inflated metrics ("index copernicus value", invented impact factors).
- Extremely fast, non-substantive peer review; spammy solicitation; hidden or
  exorbitant APCs; fake editorial boards; misleading journal names mimicking
  reputable titles.
- No DOI, or DOIs that don't resolve via Crossref.

When unsure, prefer a source that is (a) indexed in a major database and (b)
has a resolvable DOI. If neither holds, treat the claim as unverified.

## Conflict-of-interest and funding checks

- Read the **funding** and **competing interests** statements. Industry-funded
  studies are not automatically invalid, but weight them accordingly and look
  for independent replication.
- Be alert to **manufactured doubt** â€” coordinated campaigns that manufacture
  the appearance of scientific controversy (tobacco, climate, etc.). A handful
  of contrarian, industry-linked papers do not overturn a consensus built on
  the wider literature.

## Quick disposition

For each candidate source, record one of:
`EVIDENCE` (scholarly, usable) Â· `BACKGROUND` (context only) Â·
`OBJECT-OF-STUDY` (a claim being examined, not evidence) Â· `REJECT` (with reason).

**Title:** Online Plain Language Tool and Health Information Quality: A Randomized Clinical Trial

**Authors:** Julie Ayre, Carissa Bonner, Danielle M. Muscat, Erin Cvejic, Olivia Mac, Dana Mouwad, Heather L. Shepherd, Parisa Aslani, Adam G. Dunn, Kirsten J. McCaffery

**Journal:** JAMA Network Open, 2024;7(10):e2437955. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.37955 (published online October 8, 2024)

## Full abstract

> **Importance** Complex and ineffective health communication is a critical source of health inequity and occurs despite repeated policy directives to provide health information that is easy to understand and applies health literacy principles.
>
> **Objective** To evaluate the effectiveness of the Sydney Health Literacy Lab Health Literacy Editor, an easy-to-use online plain language tool that supports health information providers to apply health literacy guidelines to written health information.
>
> **Design, Setting, and Participants** This randomized clinical trial, conducted online in Australia from May 2023 to February 2024, included a convenience sample of health information providers with no previous experience using the Health Literacy Editor. Analysts were blinded to study group.
>
> **Intervention** Participants were randomized 1:1 to the intervention or control group. Participants in the intervention group were provided access to the Health Literacy Editor and a 30-minute online training program prior to editing 3 prespecified health texts. The Health Literacy Editor gives objective, real-time feedback on words and sentences. Control participants revised the texts using their own standard health information development processes.
>
> **Main Outcomes and Measures** The preregistered primary outcome was the text school grade reading score (using a validated instrument, the Simple Measure of Gobbledygook). Secondary outcomes were text complexity (percentage of text using complex language), use of passive voice (number of instances), and subjective expert ratings (5-point Likert scale corresponding to items on the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool).
>
> **Results** A total of 211 participants were randomized, with 105 in the intervention group and 106 in the control group. Of 181 participants in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean [SD] age, 41.0 [11.6] years; 154 women [85.1%]), 86 were in the intervention group and 95 in the control group. Texts revised in the intervention group had significantly improved grade reading scores (mean difference [MD], 2.48 grades; 95% CI, 1.84-3.12 grades; _P_ < .001; Cohen _d_, 0.99), lower text complexity scores (MD, 6.86; 95% CI, 4.99-8.74; _P_ < .001; Cohen _d_, 0.95), and less use of passive voice (MD, 0.95 instances; 95% CI, 0.44-1.47 instances; _P_ < .001; Cohen _d_, 0.53) compared with texts revised in the control group in intention-to-treat analyses. Experts rated texts in the intervention group more favorably for word choice and style than those in the control group (MD, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.25-0.63; _P_ < .001; Cohen _d_, 0.63), with no loss of meaning or content.
>
> **Conclusions and Relevance** In this randomized clinical trial, the Health Literacy Editor helped users simplify health information and apply health literacy guidelines to written text. The findings suggest the tool has high potential to improve development of health information for people who have low health literacy. As an online tool, the Health Literacy Editor is also easy to access and implement at scale.
>
> **Trial Registration** ANZCTR Identifier: ACTRN12623000386639

## Answers to your specific questions

- **Randomized clinical trial?** Yes â€” a 2-arm, parallel-group RCT, prospectively registered (ANZCTR: ACTRN12623000386639), with 1:1 randomization and blinded analysts.
- **Primary outcome and significance?** The preregistered primary outcome was the text school grade reading score (SMOG). It was statistically significant: intervention texts were ~2.48 grades lower (better) than control (95% CI, 1.84â€“3.12; _P_ < .001; Cohen _d_ = 0.99). In the per-protocol analysis the difference was larger: MD 3.79 grades (Cohen _d_ = 1.58).
- **What improved?** Readability grade, text complexity (fewer complex/uncommon words), passive voice (fewer instances), and expert-rated word choice and style. All secondary outcomes favored the intervention and were statistically significant.
- **Loss of content or accuracy?** No. Expert ratings for content and meaning retention were high in both groups and "did not differ significantly between the 2 groups," indicating the texts were simplified without removing key messages.
- **Effect sizes:** Cohen _d_ = 0.99 (grade reading), 0.95 (text complexity), 0.53 (passive voice), 0.63 (word choice and style) in ITT analyses â€” all large except passive voice (medium). The tool was also rated acceptable (System Usability Scale mean 70.99; perceived usefulness 3.76/5; perceived ease of use 4.03/5), though intervention participants took longer (~65 min vs ~30 min for controls).

results:
The search results identify the paper matching the query: **"The Artificial Intelligence Disclosure Penalty: Humans Persistently Devalue AI-Generated Creative Writing"** by Manav Raj (Wharton), Justin M. Berg (University of Michigan Ross), and Rob Seamans (NYU Stern), published in the *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General* (2026, DOI: 10.1037/xge0001889).

**Abstract summary (as requested):** The paper reports a series of **16 preregistered experiments** with **N = 27,491 participants** examining how evaluations of creative writing are affected by whether participants believe the content was produced with an AI model. The researchers found consistent evidence of an "AI disclosure penalty": participant evaluations of creative writing decreased when they believed writing samples were written by an AI modelâ€”or with the help of oneâ€”rather than by a human author alone. This effect is **mediated by perceived authenticity**. The penalty proved "sticky," persisting across evaluation metrics, contexts, kinds of written content, and multiple interventions derived from prior research aimed at moderating the effect. The results indicate the AI disclosure penalty is "stubbornly difficult to mitigate, at least at this time."

**Key quantitative findings:**
- **6.2% average decrease** in evaluations due to AI disclosure (Cohen's d = 0.24, a small but meaningful effect)
- Negative effect was significant in **14 of 16 studies**, with a robust meta-analytic negative relationship (p < .001)
- Total effect of AI disclosure was -0.327 (p < .001); the indirect effect through perceived authenticity was -0.292 (p < .001), while the direct effect controlling for authenticity was only -0.034 (p = .240, statistically insignificant)â€”meaning the penalty operates almost entirely through reduced perceptions of authenticity
- Authenticity strongly predicted evaluations (Î˛ = 0.611, p < .001)
- Study period spanned March 2023â€“June 2024 (15 months), using ChatGPT-generated creative writing and award-winning human-written short stories

**Failed interventions:** Researchers tested moderators derived from algorithmic aversion literatureâ€”content characteristics (narrative perspective, format, emotional tone, character humanness), evaluation context (artistic vs. utilitarian framing), information about AI capabilities, anthropomorphizing AI, and human-in-the-loop/collaboration framingâ€”and none reliably reduced the penalty. Notably, disclosing human-AI collaboration produced nearly identical negative effects as disclosing purely AI-generated content.

The research has practical implications for publishers and the U.S. Congress's consideration of the AI Disclosure Act, as mandated disclosure could reify negative biases affecting content reception and commercial viability. Lead researcher Manav Raj and colleagues noted: "Creators cannot be transparent about using AI in producing creative content without undermining appreciation for that very contentâ€”unless there are ways to reduce AI disclosure penalties."

- The study involved **16 preregistered experiments (N = 27,491 participants)** conducted between March 2023 and June 2024, using ChatGPT-generated creative writing samples.
- Results show a consistent **AI disclosure penalty**: participant evaluations of creative writing decrease when they believe content was written by an AI model â€” or with AI help â€” versus a human author alone, **mediated by perceived authenticity**.
- The penalty was **"sticky" and robust**, persisting across evaluation metrics, contexts, content types, and multiple interventions designed to moderate it (changing story perspective, humanizing the AI, framing it as collaboration, varying character type, format, emotional tone, etc.). Across all experiments, AI disclosure reduced evaluations by an average of **6.2%**.

## Replication/reproducibility aspects within the study
- **Preregistration**: All 16 experiments were preregistered, supporting methodological rigor.
- **Internal replications**: The study reports explicit replication attempts, e.g., **Study 1ca** "Replicate 1a with higher quality GPT-4 prose after mixed results" (which produced a strong penalty on all metrics), and **Study 1da** which "Replicated baseline penalty" (with a smaller effect when characters were aliens).
- The experiments were grouped into five clusters, using an iterative, exploratory approach grounded in algorithmic aversion theory, with each study informing the next.

## Robustness and implications
- The researchers state the effect is "surprisingly robust and difficult to mitigate," with Berg noting: "We threw everything at it... and nothing reliably reduced the bias."
- The results have policy implications, as the U.S. Congress considers AI disclosure legislation â€” mandated disclosure could trigger negative biases affecting reception of creative work.
- Whether the penalty will persist, diminish, or reverse as AI content becomes more pervasive remains an open question.

**Caveat**: The search results contain no evidence of an independent or conceptual replication study of this work; all replication references are to replications conducted within the 16-experiment program itself.

# Can Humans Detect AI-Generated Text Above Chance? (2024â€“2025 Findings)

The research from 2024â€“2025 paints a mixed but generally sobering picture: **most studies find that untrained humans detect AI-generated text only slightly above chance, while one notable study shows that highly experienced LLM users can be extremely accurate**.

## Laypeople perform near chance

Multiple large studies found laypeople's detection accuracy hovers near the 50% chance baseline:

- A representative study across the USA, Germany, and China (3,002 participants, CISPA, Jan 2025) found AI-generated media was nearly indistinguishable from human-created content, with participants often guessing; detection accuracy was below 50% for images and only "slightly higher" for text and audio.
- A study on news articles (1,054 participants, 2,318 judgments, testing six LLMs including GPT-4 and 7B-parameter open-weight models) found participants **could not reliably distinguish machine-generated from human-written news text** (no statistically significant difference; p > .05). This failure held across all models tested. Accuracy also degraded after roughly 30 sequential evaluations due to cognitive fatigue.
- One reported study found people could distinguish AI-generated from human-authored content only **51% of the time** â€” essentially a coin toss.
- A systematic review of 30 studies (2025â€“2026) concluded that human detection accuracy "varied widely but generally clustered around chance performance," with humans being "generally unreliable detectors."

## Experts also struggle with academic texts

A 2025 study of 63 university lecturers (engineering, economics, social sciences) evaluating 200â€“300 word excerpts from German theses found humans identified AI texts with only **57% accuracy** (vs. 50% chance), and human texts with 64% accuracy. Notably, **fewer than 20% of lecturers correctly identified professional-level AI-generated texts**. Prior teaching experience slightly improved accuracy, and there was no statistically significant difference between human and machine detector performance.

## The notable exception: experienced, frequent LLM users

A prominent study by Russell, Karpinska, and Iyyer (University of Maryland, Microsoft, UMass Amherst; arXiv:2501.15654) found that **people who frequently use LLMs for writing tasks excel at detecting AI-generated text**, even without specialized training. Key results:

- Five expert annotators (frequent LLM users) reviewing ~300 nonfiction articles achieved **99.3% accuracy at spotting AI text and 100% accuracy at identifying human text** â€” via a *majority vote* of the five annotators.
- These humans outperformed almost every commercial and open-source detector tested, with only the commercial system Pangram matching them.
- They remained accurate even against AI text that had been paraphrased or "humanized" to evade automated detectors.
- Importantly, this accuracy required a **panel of five experts** â€” individual experts were outperformed by the best automated detector, and single reviewers falsely flagged human text as AI 3.3% of the time. The authors acknowledged hiring humans is expensive and slow (~$2.82 per article, roughly a week per batch).

## Bottom line

For **laypeople and even domain experts** evaluating news, essays, or short academic texts, detection accuracy is typically only marginally above chance (51â€“57%), making unaided human detection unreliable. However, the research shows a meaningful exception: **experienced, frequent LLM users working in panels can detect AI text with near-perfect accuracy** â€” though this approach is costly, requires multiple reviewers, and may not generalize to casual readers or single evaluators.

## Summary

A 2025 study published in the *International Review of Economics Education* (Vol. 49, June 2025) by Alexandra Fiedler and JĂ¶rg DĂ¶pke examined whether human experts can identify AI-generated academic texts better than machine-based detectors.

**Study design:** The researchers conducted a survey experiment at a German university of applied sciences, asking 63 lecturers from engineering, economics, and social sciences to evaluate short excerpts (200â€“300 words) from both human-generated and AI-generated texts. The texts varied by discipline and writing level (student vs. professional).

**Key findings:**
- **Humans detected AI-generated texts at only 57% accuracy** â€” just slightly better than random chance (50% baseline) â€” and correctly identified human-generated texts 64% of the time.
- AI detectors performed comparably; there was **no statistically significant difference between human and machine performance**.
- **Professional-level AI texts were nearly undetectable**, with fewer than 20% of respondents correctly classifying them.
- Prior teaching experience slightly improved recognition accuracy, according to regression analyses.
- Subjective judgments of text quality were not influenced by actual or presumed authorship â€” meaning evaluators could not tell whether a text was AI-generated based on perceived quality.

**Conclusions:** The authors warn that current written examination practices are increasingly vulnerable to undetected AI use, as both human judgment and existing AI detectors show high error rates, especially for high-quality AI-generated content. They conclude that a reconsideration of traditional assessment formats in academia is warranted.

# Summary: "Is it Cake or is it AI? A Systematic Review of Human Uncertainty in Distinguishing Generative Artificial Intelligence Content"

## Overview
This systematic review by Mark Louie F. Ramos (arXiv:2604.03437, submitted April 3, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2604.03437) synthesizes empirical evidence on humans' ability to distinguish generative AI (gen AI) content from human-produced content across **text, image, and voice modalities**. It was cross-listed in Applications (stat.AP) and Computers and Society (cs.CY).

## Methodology
- A structured search of **Scopus identified 22,541 records from 2025 to 2026**; of these, **1,200 were screened** and **30 studies were included**.
- Screening followed **PRISMA guidelines**.
- Inclusion required empirical measurement of human detection accuracy with clearly reported or reconstructible classification proportions.
- The review intentionally avoids meta-analytic effect sizes due to methodological diversity and instead presents a **descriptive synthesis** of detection tasks spanning voice, image, narrative, technical, and media text content.

## Key Findings
**Overall conclusion:** Human detection accuracy varied widely but **generally clustered around chance performance** â€” humans are generally unreliable detectors of gen AI content.

- **Chance-level performance across studies:** In the majority of studies (17 of 30, n = 2,285), detection accuracy clustered tightly around random guessing (range: 28%â€“67%); in several studies, pooled accuracy was statistically indistinguishable from 50%.
- **Voice modality (strongest):** All three voice-focused studies reported above-chance detection, with accuracy as high as **75.4%**, attributed to subtle acoustic artifacts (timing, pitch, prosody). However, fine-grained discrimination was often not replicable across populations.
- **Image modality:** Human accuracy often **dipped below chance** (e.g., identifying AI-generated faces) or hovered near 50%, with exceptions only where salient visual heuristics (unnatural reflections, impossible lighting) were present.
- **Text modality:** Only **2 of 24 text-related results** showed statistically significant above-chance accuracy, both tied to narrative media content where participants were explicitly aware AI might be involved. Technical/evaluative contexts (academic manuscripts, application statements, scientific reports, translation tasks) showed **no meaningful deviation from chance**.
- **Expertise effect:** Domain expertise did not consistently improve classification; experienced reviewers and professional evaluators often showed uncertainty similar to lay participants.

## Implications and Strong Claims
- Human capacity to detect gen AI content is **generally unreliable and inconsistent**, with only sporadic subgroups (mainly voice, sometimes narrative text) performing above chance.
- **Rhetorical polish or linguistic sophistication is invalid as an evaluative criterion** for authorship or merit â€” a direct challenge to traditional evaluation heuristics in academic and application contexts.

## Summary: Fiedler & DĂ¶pke (2025), *International Review of Economics Education*

**Bibliographic details:** Alexandra Fiedler and JĂ¶rg DĂ¶pke, "Do humans identify AI-generated text better than machines? Evidence based on excerpts from German theses," *International Review of Economics Education*, Vol. 49, Article 100321 (2025). DOI: 10.1016/j.iree.2025.100321. It is an open-access article published under a Creative Commons license.

**Research design:** The authors conducted a survey experiment at a German university of applied sciences. Sixty-three lecturers in engineering, economics, and social sciences were asked to evaluate short excerpts (200â€“300 words) drawn from both human-generated and AI-generated texts. The texts varied by discipline and writing level (student vs. professional).

**Key findings:**
- **Neither humans nor machines perform well:** Both human evaluators and AI detectors correctly identified AI-generated texts only slightly better than chance. Humans achieved a recognition rate of **57% for AI-generated texts** and **64% for human-generated texts** â€” meaning only about half of AI texts were correctly flagged as AI-generated.
- **No significant humanâ€“machine difference:** There was no statistically significant difference between human and machine performance, although humans recognized AI texts slightly better than AI detectors (per the article's highlights).
- **Professional-level AI text is hardest to detect:** Professional-level AI-generated texts were the most difficult to identify, with **fewer than 20% of respondents correctly classifying them**.
- **Experience helps only marginally:** Regression analyses suggest that prior teaching experience slightly improves recognition accuracy.
- **Quality judgments are unaffected by authorship:** Subjective judgments of text quality were not influenced by actual or presumed authorship.

**Conclusions:** The findings indicate that current written examination practices are increasingly vulnerable to undetected AI use, as both human judgment and existing AI detectors show high error rates â€” especially for high-quality AI-generated content. The authors conclude that a reconsideration of traditional assessment formats in academia is warranted. The paper is categorized with keywords "Artificial Intelligence," "Written examinations," and "Grading," and is classified under JEL codes A2, I23, and C88.

**Answer to the research question:** Based on this study, humans do **not** identify AI-generated text meaningfully better than machines â€” both perform only slightly above chance, with no statistically significant difference between them, and high-quality (professional-level) AI text is nearly impossible for human experts to detect.

# Summary: "ChatGPT Text Products and Their Linguistic Correctness" by Jolanta Mazurkiewicz-SokoĹ‚owska (ECAI 2025)

## Publication Details
- **Author:** Jolanta Mazurkiewicz-SokoĹ‚owska, University of Szczecin, Poland
- **Published in:** *Emerging Challenges in Intelligent Management Information Systems* (ECAI 2025), Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems, vol. 1643, Springer, Cham (pp. 250â€“265, 16 pages)
- **DOI:** 10.1007/978-3-032-06611-4_20

## Research Focus
The paper examines ChatGPT's language capabilities specifically regarding **text cohesion**, providing a comparative qualitative and quantitative analysis of grammatical and lexical correctness (including spelling and punctuation) in **three languages: English, German, and Polish**. The study aims to identify linguistic deficiencies in ChatGPT's text products and discuss the limits of **chain-of-thought (CoT)** reasoning regarding opportunities to improve ChatGPT's linguistic agility.

## Methodology and Research Material
The study was designed to trigger non-standard ChatGPT responses, since pilot studies showed ChatGPT translates almost flawlessly and produces coherent texts on given topics. The task posed was a **metaphorical question about "colours of love"**, requiring unusual but contextually appropriate solutions.

The research corpus comprises **480 ChatGPT answers total (160 per language)**:
- **300 expressions** (100 per language) â€” colours of love generated by ChatGPT
- **180 descriptions** (150 explanations, 50 per language) â€” 5 explanations for each of 10 randomly chosen expressions with the most unconventional meanings per language
- **30 short stories** (10 per language) â€” "verbal pictures" for each of the 10 analysed expressions per language

The 10 analysed expressions per language included unconventional creations such as:
- **English:** antique lace, cotton candy, electric fuchsia, forever blue, chartreuse glow, obsidian ache, indigo intuition, confetti heart, deep smoke, bluebell wish
- **German:** PopcornweiĂź (popcorn white), MagentagefĂĽhl (magenta feeling), GranatapfelsĂĽĂźe (pomegranate sweetness), Nachtviolett (night violet), etc.
- **Polish:** lazurowa bliskoĹ›Ä‡ (azure closeness), pomaraĹ„czowy entuzjazm (orange enthusiasm), cynamonowa namiÄ™tnoĹ›Ä‡ (cinnamon passion), grafitowa lojalnoĹ›Ä‡ (graphite loyalty), etc.

All 300 expressions were analysed according to the criterion of **presence of a colour name**, divided into types: expressions containing colour names (e.g., "forever blue," "Tiefschwarz"), names referring to colours via food products (e.g., "burnt sugar," "PfirsichwĂ¤rme," "miodowy spokĂłj"), and names of metals, stones, minerals, or ceramic (e.g., "obsidian ache," "Bernsteinseele," "bursztyn nostalgii").

## Paper Structure
1. **Section 1** â€” ChatGPT's capabilities and limitations
2. **Section 2** â€” Textuality criteria, highlighting cohesion as essential (cohesion as a basic indicator of "the unity and texture" of a text)
3. **Section 3** â€” Materials and methods
4. **Section 4** â€” Results and discussion

## Key Findings
The results show that **the impact of chain-of-thought can still be recognized in overused linguistic constructions** in ChatGPT's generated text products.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** Why Does ChatGPT "Delve" So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models

**Authors:** Tom S. Juzek and Zina B. Ward

**Year:** 2025

**Venue:** COLING (31st International Conference on Computational Linguistics)

## Abstract
"Scientific English is currently undergoing rapid change, with words like 'delve,' 'intricate,' and 'underscore' appearing far more frequently than just a few years ago." The researchers developed a method identifying 21 focal words likely overused due to LLM adoption and investigated their origins.

## Conclusions on Source

The paper found **no clear single cause**:

- **Ruled out:** Model architecture, algorithm choices, and training data showed "no evidence" of causing the overrepresentation
- **Partially implicated:** RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) showed some consistency with involvement, though the evidence remained inconclusive
- **Remains uncertain:** "insights into the workings of LLMs are within reach, a lack of transparency surrounding model development remains an obstacle"

## Human Preferences

Notably, the study's "exploratory online study" suggested "participants may be reacting differently to 'delve' than to other focal words," implying inconsistent human preference patterns across overused terms rather than uniform preference for such language.

Based on the search results, I found the study you're looking for. Here's what I found about the research:

Jiang, Yang; Hao, Jiangang; Fauss, Michael; Li, Chen published "Detecting ChatGPT-Generated Essays in a Large-Scale Writing Assessment: Is there a Bias Against Non-Native English Speakers?" in Computers & Education, v217 in August 2024.

The study leveraged well-sampled large-scale data from the GRE writing assessment to systematically investigate the potential bias of methods for detecting ChatGPT-generated essays against or in favor of native and non-native English speakers.

Key findings from the research include:

- Detectors based on e-rater and/or perplexity features performed very well in detecting ChatGPT-generated text.

- The study addressed research questions about how essays written by native and non-native English speakers and ChatGPT-generated essays differ in text perplexity and writing quality, how well detectors based on linguistic features and text perplexity can detect ChatGPT-generated essays, and whether there is bias in the detectors against or in favor of non-native English speakers compared to native English speakers.

It's worth noting that this 2024 study by Jiang et al. represents a follow-up to earlier research that had raised concerns about bias against non-native speakers in AI detectors.

I've completed the web search for your query about the Polish Language Council's spelling and punctuation rules changes effective from January 1, 2026.

## Key Findings:

The changes to Polish spelling rules effective from January 1, 2026 include capitalization of names of city inhabitants and their districts, neighborhoods and villages, such as Warszawianin, Zgierzanin, Ochocianka, Mokotowianin, Nowohucianin, ChochoĹ‚owianin.

The changes announced in the press release from May 10, 2024 concern some rules for using capital and lowercase letters, as well as connected or separate spelling and hyphenation usage. Their purpose is to unify rules and make them easier for writers to learn and apply in practice.

The Council announced the document titled "Zasady pisowni i interpunkcji polskiej" (Rules of Polish Spelling and Punctuation), which from January 1, 2026 will become the only authoritative source of orthographic and punctuation rules.

To give all persons and institutions, especially publishers, dictionary authors and school program developers, time to prepare for the new situation, the Council decided that the adopted changes would take effect from January 1, 2026.
